title: Numbers and prices: bargaining at Talat Sao
goal: Count to a million, ask prices, bargain without sounding rude, and say long kip amounts the way locals do.
bekal: numbers 1–1,000,000, including the ເອັດ and ຊາວ traps

dialogs.title: ບົດສົນທະນາ — At a fabric stall, Talat Sao
dialogs.intro: Budi is bargaining for a scarf. Notice the rhythm: in Laos, bargaining is done gently, with a smile, and almost always gets the price down a little — but don't offer half the price the way you might at some markets elsewhere.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສະບາຍດີ|Sa-baai-dii] [ອັນ|An][ນີ້|nîi][ເທົ່າໃດ|thao-dai]
lines.id: Hello. How much is this one?

lines.speaker: ແມ່ຄ້າ:
lines.text: [ແປດ|Pèet][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán][ກີບ|kìip]

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ໂອ້ຍ|Ôoy] [ແພງ|Pheeng][ຫຼາຍ|lǎai][ເນາະ|nāw] [ຫຼຸດ|Lut][ແດ່|dèe][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw]
lines.id: Oh, that's expensive. Can you lower it a bit?
lines.literal: oh. expensive — much — isn't-it? lower — a-bit — can — (question)?

lines.speaker: ແມ່ຄ້າ:
lines.text: [ເຈົ້າ|Jâo] [ເອົາ|Ao][ຈັກ|ják][ຜືນ|phʉ̌ʉn]
lines.id: Sure. How many do you want?

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ສອງ|Sǎwng][ຜືນ|phʉ̌ʉn] [ຖ້າ|Thàa][ເອົາ|ao][ສອງ|sǎwng][ຜືນ|phʉ̌ʉn] [ເທົ່າໃດ|thao-dai]
lines.id: Two. If I take two, how much?
lines.literal: two — piece. if — take — two — piece — how-much?

lines.speaker: ແມ່ຄ້າ:
lines.text: [ໜຶ່ງ|Nʉ̀ng][ແສນ|sěen][ຫ້າ|hāa][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán] [ລາຄາ|Láa-kháa][ພິເສດ|phi-sèet][ເດີ້|dòe]
lines.id: A hundred and fifty thousand. A special price, okay?
lines.literal: one — hundred-thousand — five — ten — thousand. price — special — okay.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ໜຶ່ງ|Nʉ̀ng][ແສນ|sěen][ສາມ|sǎam][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán][ໄດ້|dâi][ບໍ່|bàw] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຊິ|si][ມາ|maa][ຊື້|sʉ̂ʉ][ອີກ|ìik]
lines.id: Would a hundred and thirty thousand work? I'll come back and buy more.
lines.literal: one — hundred-thousand — three — ten — thousand — can — (question)? I — will — come — buy — again.

lines.speaker: ແມ່ຄ້າ:
lines.text: [ໂອ|Ôo] [ໜຶ່ງ|nʉ̀ng][ແສນ|sěen][ສີ່|sìi][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán][ເນາະ|nāw] [ບໍ່|Bàw][ໄດ້|dâi][ກຳໄລ|kam-lái][ແລ້ວ|lèeo]
lines.id: Oh… a hundred and forty thousand, okay? I'm not making a profit anymore.
lines.literal: oh. one — hundred-thousand — four — ten — thousand — isn't-it? not — get — profit — already.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ໄດ້|Dâi] [ເອົາ|Ao][ເລີຍ|lóei] [ຂ້ອຍ|Khàwy][ຈ່າຍ|jàai][ເງິນ|ngóen][ສົດ|sót]
lines.id: Okay, I'll take them. I'll pay cash.
lines.literal: can. take — right-away. I — pay — money — fresh.

lines.speaker: ແມ່ຄ້າ:
lines.text: [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai][ຫຼາຍໆ|lǎai-lǎai] [ນີ້|Nîi][ເງິນ|ngóen][ທອນ|thawn][ຫົກ|hók][ສິບ|síp][ພັນ|phán]
lines.id: Thank you very much. Here's your change, sixty thousand.
lines.literal: thank-you — much-much. this — money — return — six — ten — thousand.

lines.speaker: ບູດີ:
lines.text: [ຖືກ|Thʉ̀ʉk][ແລ້ວ|lèeo] [ຂອບໃຈ|Khàwp-jai][ເດີ້| dòe] [ພົບ|Phop][ກັນ|kan][ໃໝ່|mài]
lines.id: That's right. Thank you. See you again.
lines.literal: right — already. thank-you — (friendly). meet — together — new.

notes: **ເທົ່າໃດ thao-dai is the one word you must memorize today.** It means "how much/how many" for prices and amounts, and it goes at the **end**: *ອັນນີ້ເທົ່າໃດ* (how much is this?). Pointing at things while saying it is enough to shop all day.

**Kip amounts always sound long, so people shorten them.** 80,000 is said *pèet-síp-phán* (eighty thousand), but at the market people often just say *pèet-síp* — and both sides know it means thousands. If in doubt, repeat the full number; the seller will nod or correct you.

**ຫຼຸດ lut = "lower, cut," and ຫຼຸດແດ່ໄດ້ບໍ່ is the standard bargaining sentence.** The little *ແດ່ dèe* in the middle is what makes it polite — without it, the sentence sounds like an order. Compare "lower it" with "could you lower it a little?"

**ຈັກ ják also means "how many," but it's used WITH a classifier.** *ຈັກຜືນ* (how many pieces), *ຈັກຄົນ* (how many people), *ຈັກໂມງ* (what time). *ເທົ່າໃດ* is for amounts without a counting unit: money, weight, age.

**ເອົາ ao = "take, want, I'll buy it."** It's the most important verb at the market. *ເອົາອັນນີ້* (I'll take this one), *ບໍ່ເອົາ* (no thanks, I don't want it). Said on its own, *ເອົາ* means "yes, I'll take it."
**ຖ້າ thàa = "if."** It goes in front of the condition, just like English: *ຖ້າເອົາສອງຜືນ…* (if I take two…). No linking word is required in the next clause.

**ເລີຍ lóei means "right away, in that case" and smooths a decision.** *ເອົາເລີຍ* = "okay then, I'll take it." This word shows up everywhere in Lao conversation and is hard to translate exactly; just feel that it closes the deal.
**ຖືກ thʉ̀ʉk has two meanings: "cheap" and "correct."** *ລາຄາຖືກ* (the price is cheap), *ຖືກແລ້ວ* (that's right, that's exact). Context separates them, and both are equally common.

**Bargaining etiquette in Laos.** Bargain once, twice at most, and stop. Haggling endlessly or naming a number far below makes the seller go quiet and lose face — and in Lao culture, making someone lose face is much worse than losing money. If the price won't budge, smile, say *ຂອບໃຈເດີ້*, and walk on; that's polite and hurts no one.

grammars.title: Numbers: the pattern, and two traps you must memorize
after: **Trap 1: a final "1" becomes ເອັດ *ét* after tens.** 11 = *síp-ét*, not *síp-nʉ̀ng*. The same goes for 21, 31, 101, 1,001 — all *-ét*.
**Trap 2: 20 is a word of its own.** *ຊາວ saao*, not *sǎwng-síp*. Only 20 works like this; 30 through 90 follow the regular pattern.
For big numbers, read from the largest unit: 150,000 = *nʉ̀ng-sěen hāa-síp-phán* (one hundred-thousand, fifty thousand). It looks complicated on paper and sounds perfectly normal after a few days.

sections.title: Money, and saying the numbers like a local

blocks.text: Notice how "one" **moves to the end**: *ແສນໜຶ່ງ sěen nʉ̀ng* sounds more natural than *ໜຶ່ງແສນ*. The same rule applies to classifiers: *ຈອກໜຶ່ງ jàwk nʉ̀ng* (a cup), not *ໜຶ່ງຈອກ*.
In the big cities, US dollars and Thai baht also circulate in large stores and hotels: *ໂດລາ doo-laa*, *ບາດ bàat*. At markets and food stalls, kip is the only currency used.

sections.title: Adjectives for judging prices and goods

blocks.text: Adjectives come **after** the noun, the opposite of English: *ຜ້າງາມ phàa ngáam* (beautiful cloth), *ລາຄາແພງ láa-kháa pheeng* (expensive price). And adjectives don't need a verb "to be": *ຜ້າງາມ* already means "the cloth is beautiful."
